classification_signals: Extensive citations to other research (e.g., Stoller, Classen, Hall, Gibson, Reber, Mishima, Burckhardt) throughout the text (pp. 2-33).
No explicit 'Methods', 'Results', or 'Discussion' sections for a new empirical study.
The paper builds a conceptual argument by synthesizing existing knowledge across disciplines like anthropology, psychology, and history.
The 'Conclusion' section (p. 31) summarizes the theoretical points made in the paper.
title: Perception and Material Culture: Historical and Cross-Cultural Perspectives

findings.consequent: Human perception
findings.quote: Human perception is a matter of tradition, permeated with history and culture.

findings.consequent: Nexus of perception, history, and culture (body as key site where nature/culture, material/mental, individual/collective meet)
findings.quote: Material culture is especially important in the nexus of perception, history and culture, and the body is the key site where nature and culture

findings.antecedent: Learning (perceptual learning, cultural learning), biology (species-specific physiology, unfinished nature)
findings.consequent: Human perception (saturation, restriction, completion)
findings.quote: human perception is nevertheless saturated with learning. Our biology necessitates perceptual learning to restrict and complete its originally

findings.consequent: Evidence of bygone perceptual reality
findings.quote: Historical artifacts and texts give evidence of bygone perceptual reality, but what people said about their perceptions, and our interpretations

findings.consequent: Historical variability of perception
findings.quote: If perception is culturally variable, it is historically variable as well.

findings.antecedent: Intersubjective experience of the perceived world
findings.consequent: Difficulty imagining discordant perceptions in others
findings.quote: the world each of us perceives is so obviously there (and so obviously there, intersubjectively, for so many people), that it is hard to imagine

findings.consequent: Difficulty imagining experiences in another culture
findings.quote: we are each so enmeshed in our own culture that it is quite difficult to even imagine the experiences we might have in another culture.

findings.antecedent: Deep immersion in Songhay culture (ethnographic experience)
findings.consequent: Realization of inseparability of thought, feeling, and action
findings.quote: Slowly, I uncovered an important rule: one cannot separate thought from feeling and action; they are inextricably linked.

findings.consequent: Importance of taste, smell, hearing (over sight) for understanding material culture
findings.quote: taste, smell, and hearing are often more important for the Songhay than sight, the privileged sense of the West.

findings.consequent: Perceived world organized by sound and kinaesthesia (pulsating auditory environment)
findings.quote: the perceived world and its attendant meanings are not organized according to the primary modality of sight, as in Euro-America, but according to sound and kinaesthesia.

findings.consequent: Avoidance of 'startle' (abruptness, especially auditory/kinaesthetic/ethical) to prevent separation of human soul from host
findings.quote: Temiar life is organized to avoid "startle"-that abruptness, especially auditory but also kinaesthetic or ethical-that can separate a human soul from its host.

findings.consequent: Heat as predominant perceptual mode, organizing daily life and cosmological meaning
findings.quote: For the Tzotzil of the Chiapas highlands in Mexico, heat is the predominant perceptual mode, organizing both daily life and cosmological meaning.

findings.consequent: Diminished importance of smell, increased hegemony of sight over sensory experience
findings.quote: smell has diminished in importance as sight increasingly has established hegemony over sensory experience.

findings.consequent: Scent removed from experience and relegated to conceptual insignificance
findings.quote: By the late 19th century, scent had not only been largely removed from experience, but it had been relegated to an arena of conceptual insignificance

findings.consequent: Advancing evolution, increasing cultural sophistication, and mental health (as argued by Darwin and others)
findings.quote: Darwin and others argued that the declining ability to smell was a hallmark of advancing evolution, of increasing cultural sophistication and, for some, a sign of mental health.

findings.consequent: Cultivation of sense of smell, organization of calendar and space by odor
findings.quote: the Andaman Islanders cultivate their sense of smell and organize large parts of their lives around it. The Andaman calendar is structured by odor

findings.consequent: Experience of space as a dynamic environmental flow (contrasting with static Euro-American experience)
findings.quote: Andamans do not experience space "as a static area within which things happen, but more as a dynamic environmental flow."

findings.antecedent: African culture (perceptual structures, material forms, cosmological insights - 'philosophemes')
findings.consequent: Persistence in the Americas despite profound disruptions
findings.quote: African culture preserved by the slaves' descendants flowed into the mainstreams of the developing North and South American cultures.

findings.consequent: Deep embedding and intellectual/sensuous appreciation in American cultures
findings.quote: African derived philosophemes are deeply embedded in the life of various cultures in the Americas, as Thompson says, they are "intellectually perceived and sensuously appreciated".

findings.antecedent: Continuities in material culture (e.g., Yoruba orisha, Kongolese cosmograms, Mande architecture)
findings.consequent: Preservation of African ways of experiencing the world in African-American communities
findings.quote: African ways of experiencing the world, and the values associated with them, have been kept alive in African-American communities through continuities in material culture

findings.consequent: Emphasis on interpenetration of functions and interrelation of persons (contrasting with grid-formed European architecture)
findings.quote: the round houses emphasize interpenetration of functions and interrelation of persons.

findings.consequent: Families kept together in socially binding spaces
findings.quote: Mali-derived round houses "keep families together in socially binding spaces."

findings.antecedent: Bodies of slaves (as site of culture transference)
findings.consequent: Fundamental existence of culture in the body (first artifact of material culture)
findings.quote: The transference of African culture to the New World in the naked, possessionless bodies of slaves denotes the fundamental existence of culture in the body, which is the first artifact of material culture

findings.consequent: Global (pertaining to the whole), synaesthetic (involving all senses), and somatic (incorporating body feelings/capacities with world perceptions) nature
findings.quote: Our perception is global (pertaining to the whole, rather than its parts), synaesthetic (involving all the senses at once), and somatic (incorporating perceptions of my body, its feelings and capacities with perceptions of the world in which my body finds itself).

findings.consequent: Acquisition of rich subtlety of adult experience
findings.quote: Through our developing perception of the world, including our own being in the world, we acquire the rich subtlety of adult experience.

findings.consequent: Tied to an ability to act in the environment, involving proprioception, kinaesthesia, and environmental perception
findings.quote: Like any animal's perception, ours is tied to an ability to act in the environment, involving and integrating proprioception (the body's experience of itself) and kinaesthesia (the body's experience of itself as moving or able to move), as well as environmental perception (the body's experience of the external world).

findings.consequent: Manifestation of intense self-interest in the pragmatic relationship between the animal and its world (not innately disinterested)
findings.quote: Perception is not innately disinterested, but manifests an intense self-interest in the pragmatic relationship between the animal and its world.

findings.consequent: Perception as inherent connection to self, world, and potential for action ('possibility for itself in the world')
findings.quote: The amoeba has experienced a potential for itself in the world (food) and acted on the information by eating through a concatenation of its proprioception (need for food), environmental information (availability of food) and kinaesthesia (moving to surround). This is not stimulus/response; the animal perceives a "possibility for itself in the world" and is always already in touch with its self, its world, and its potential for action.

findings.consequent: Perception (enabling animal survival and thriving)
findings.quote: Perception evolves so that a perceiving animal can survive and, beyond that, thrive.

findings.consequent: Function as systems for exploring, searching, and selecting ambient energy
findings.quote: The senses are best understood as systems for exploring, searching and selecting ambient energy.

findings.consequent: Part of sensitivity (not a separate act of the mind upon sensory input)
findings.quote: Attention is part of sensitivity, not a separate act of the mind upon sensory input.

findings.consequent: Affordances (environmental relevances determined from the locus of the perceiving animal)
findings.quote: Information-for-an-animal exemplifies James Gibson's idea of "affordance," which refers to environmental relevances, determined from the locus of the perceiving animal.

findings.consequent: Information about how, where, and when aspects of the world can affect or be affected by the animal, rooting all significance in this perceptual base
findings.quote: the synaesthetic array of affordances tells the animal how, where and when aspects of the world can affect or be affected by it. All significance takes root from this perceptual base.

findings.consequent: Possible actions involving the perceiver and her environment (including actions not yet undertaken)
findings.quote: Affordances correspond to possible actions involving the perceiver and her environment. [We see] not only objects and their properties but events as well. We see ourselves, too, and our own actions and movements; we can even see the possibility of actions that we have not actually undertaken. Such possibilities are called "affordances"

findings.consequent: Animal attention to relevant aspects of the world, perception (significance as key at all levels)
findings.quote: Animals attend to those aspects of the world that hold relevance for our biological well-being. Significance is the key to perception at all levels.

findings.consequent: Orientation toward possibilities most relevant to the animal's well-being
findings.quote: Successful perceptual strategies are oriented toward possibilities that are in fact most relevant to the animal's well-being.

findings.consequent: Perception (inherently shaped simultaneously)
findings.quote: Perception is inherently shaped simultaneously by the animal's desire and capacity, on the one hand, and by the possibilities presented by the world, on the other.

findings.consequent: Planning (manifested by perception, improved by learning)
findings.quote: Perception manifests a sort of planning, and learning gives evidence of improved planning.

findings.consequent: Informed perceptual matrix, improved behaviors and perception of relevant affordances (even in simple animals)
findings.quote: Perceptual intelligence informs all elements of the perceptual matrix. Even very simple animals, like plenaria and earthworms, learn: they get better at repeated behaviors (skill improvement); they get better at perceiving relevant affordances (learning about the world); and they develop new behaviors that lead to new skills and new affordances.

findings.consequent: Dimension of meaningfulness and abstraction, always already significant and folded into a world organization
findings.quote: Perception, then, has a dimension of meaningfulness and a level of abstraction. What I perceive is always already significant to me and folded into the organization of a world to which I belong and which has meaning for me.

findings.consequent: Categorization and abstraction (perceptual abstraction)
findings.quote: Perception requires complex categorization. Even for the amoeba, perceiving "food" involves categorization and thus abstraction (not yet conceptual, but perceptual abstraction).

findings.consequent: Interested character of conception (as cognition evolves out of proto-logos of perceptual intelligence)
findings.quote: The notion of affordance displays the "interested" character of perception, a character which must apply to conception, too, if it is a result of natural selection. Cognition evolves out of the proto-logos of perceptual intelligence, further developing the dimension of significance displayed in perception.

findings.consequent: Purpose of surviving, thriving, reproducing, and regenerating the species (not 'truth')
findings.quote: The purpose of cognition is not "truth"-cognitive models intended to describe the "real" world. Animal behavior is not attuned to "reality itself," but first to surviving, then to thriving, and always to reproducing and regenerating the species.

findings.consequent: Evolutionary phenomena naturally selected for ability to help animals and groups survive and thrive in complex situations
findings.quote: Cognition, reason, theory and modeling are evolutionary phenomena naturally selected for their ability to help animals and groups of animals survive and thrive in complex situations.

findings.antecedent: Hominid evolution (increasing infant brain size, lengthening neoteny, increasingly complex tool kit)
findings.consequent: Emergence of socially-shared cognitive models (e.g., Homo erectus)
findings.quote: Somewhere in the course of evolution hominids came to need socially-shared cognitive models as part of the development that led, somewhat later, to the appearance of speech. The gradually increasing need for shared cognitive models corresponded with increasing infant brain size, lengthening neoteny and an increasingly complex tool kit.

findings.antecedent: Domestication of fire, complex rule-driven toolmaking
findings.consequent: Indication of species able to develop sophisticated theories to guide multistep actions, remember them, and teach them to succeeding generations
findings.quote: The domestication of fire and the appearance of complex, rule-driven toolmaking indicate a species able to develop sophisticated theories to guide and refine multistep actions, to remember them (the actions and theories) and to teach them to succeeding generations.

findings.consequent: Enhanced gradual development of material culture, transformed structure and content of the perceptual world (olfactory, auditory, visual, kinaesthetic, proprioceptive changes)
findings.quote: Fire greatly enhanced the gradual development of material culture, which itself began once toolmaking was transmitted across generations. ... Material culture, actively generated with physical skills, guided by intellectual attainments, and taught from generation to generation, began to transform the structure and content of the perceptual world, affecting kinaesthesia (through skill development), environmental perception (transforming the physical environment by permeating it with artifacts and built environments), and proprioception (through the transformation of kinaesthesia and environmental perception).

findings.antecedent: Ability to learn and teach new skills (related to material culture)
findings.consequent: Factors in natural selection, enhancing survival through coordinated behavior and shared perceptual experiences
findings.quote: At the same time, the ability to learn and teach these new skills became factors in natural selection (as, of course, did the actual usefulness of the skills and plans). Survival depended in part on coordinated behavior, while behavioral coordination required actors to have correlated perceptual experiences and shared structures of meaning.

findings.consequent: Transformation of the material world and creation of material culture (pragmatic and semiotic things, spaces, places, times, physicalities) to effect coordinated economic and ecological behavior
findings.quote: hominids transformed the material world and created material culture-making things, spaces, places, times and other physicalities that were at once pragmatic and semiotic.

findings.consequent: Transmission of patterns of behavior, meaning, and experience (including techniques for structuring perceptual experience), enhancing group vitality and survival
findings.quote: Cultures transmit patterns of behavior, meaning and experience across generations; successful cultures enhance group vitality and survival. Techniques and patterns for structuring perceptual experience are among the processes taught intergenerationally.

findings.antecedent: Species-specific variation, cultural plasticity, extreme neoteny
findings.consequent: Capacity to vary from one another (culturally, individually)
findings.quote: one of our species-specific characteristics, connecting us with one another and distinguishing us from other species, is our capacity to vary from one another, from group to group (culturally) and from person to person (individually). One of our cross-cultural resemblances is our extreme neoteny, which is at once a source and a product of our cultural plasticity.

findings.antecedent: Maturational processes, physical/social/cultural contexts, adult teaching/guidance
findings.consequent: Children's 'completion' (development to functional adulthood)
findings.quote: "completion" through maturational processes that take place in and are affected by physical, social and cultural contexts. Not only do children have important relationships with adults; adults stay in profound relationships with children for an extended period as well. Considerable time and significant resources must be devoted to teaching and guidance throughout the maturational process.

findings.consequent: Structured time and space, created objects, relationships, rhythms, social forms, and environmental exchanges that make up the content of the infant's external world
findings.quote: culture structures time and space while creating objects, sets of relationships, rhythms, social forms, and environmental exchanges which make up the content of the infant's external world.

findings.consequent: Multisensory, embodied experience of the world (haptically, visually, olfactorily, with whole bodies, movements, social/physical surroundings)
findings.quote: From the beginning, we experience the world haptically, visually, olfactorily. Infants' whole bodies are involved including their movements and their social and physical surroundings.

findings.consequent: Perception (not value-neutral, intimately bound)
findings.quote: "[P]erception is not value-neutral: everywhere the sensory order is bound up with the cultural order in intimate ways."

findings.consequent: Material culture (encompassing everything physical shaped by culture: tools, clothing, transportation, bodily skills, architecture, arts, ritual, texts, speech)
findings.quote: Everything physical which has been shaped by culture belongs to material culture, encompassing everything from salt shakers to sacred mountains, home environments to international transportation routes. It incorporates all that is physical in culture, including tools, clothing, transportation, bodily skills, architecture, arts and ritual. It even includes texts (insofar as they exist physically in books, documents, letters and so forth) and speech (insofar as some determinate sound is spoken and heard).

findings.consequent: Interactions with and through material culture
findings.quote: For the greater part of nearly every day most of our interactions are with and through material culture.

findings.antecedent: Human transformation of physical world (material culture)
findings.consequent: Altered relationship between perception and the human environment, leading to cultural landscapes where most objects are artifacts
findings.quote: Our spectacular transformation of the physical world has altered the relationship between perception and the human environment. We no longer live in predominantly "natural" landscapes provided by extra-human entities and processes, but largely in cultural landscapes where most objects are artifacts and most processes and relationships are humanly produced.

findings.consequent: Organized worlds of shared experience, deep perceptual process involvement, generation of cross-cultural differences
findings.quote: Cultures are constrained by the physical world, our bodies' possibilities and limits, and the biological potentials and dangers of a given location. Within these constraints our neoteny and the richness of the world's infinite affordances give rise to considerable flexibility as cultures organize worlds of shared experience in which people of all ages can cooperate to sustain and reproduce life. This process reaches deep into the perceptual process. Its functioning and the cross-cultural differences it generates are important, especially in periods of cultural contact and mixing such as our own.

findings.consequent: Limited perceptual field to manageable affordances, unconsciousness of constant or regular elements
findings.quote: One important technique is habituation: we tend to become unconscious of constant or regular elements of the perceptual world, whether they originate in our bodies (as practices and skills) or in the world (as environmental regularities).

findings.consequent: Frustrating conscious processes, sudden improvements and plateaus, decreased conscious involvement over time (skill mastery)
findings.quote: Although we try to remember the right information about a skill at the right time, it is not possible to do so at first. ... Our progress toward skill mastery is marked by sudden improvements followed by plateaus in which little improvement is noticed, and, in fact, performance may slightly decline. With practice and attention another period of improvement comes until we learn the skill. By this point, our conscious processes are hardly involved at all

findings.antecedent: Early infancy learning, basic physical skills (e.g., sitting, walking)
findings.consequent: Cultural variability, correlation with specific material cultures, unconscious acquisition
findings.quote: Many of the skills we learn in early infancy derive from the context provided by material culture. Even basic physical skills such as sitting up, rolling over and walking are culturally variable and correlated with specific material cultures. These and other habituated skills are acquired in infancy and forgotten to consciousness.

findings.consequent: Newborn movement synchrony, forming a template for sophisticated rhythmic/temporal experiences and speech acquisition
findings.quote: William Condon found that newborn babies synchronize their spastic movements with speech, perhaps as early as the first hour of life, and they do so in a well-developed fashion by the second day. ... This early temporal patterning probably forms the template on which more sophisticated rhythmic and temporal experiences are constructed, and almost surely forms one of the bases of speech acquisition.

findings.antecedent: Maturation, practice of predominant cultural rhythms
findings.consequent: Inability to synchronize with other rhythms
findings.quote: as they mature they begin to practice the rhythms that predominate in their enculturation. They become unable to synchronize with other rhythms.

findings.consequent: Communication failure ('out of synch')
findings.quote: When people who have habituated differing rhythmic structures attempt to communicate, they may fail because they are literally "out of synch."

findings.consequent: Introjection of body experiences (locomotion, posture, rhythm), body as artifact saturated with material culture
findings.quote: Thus fundamental experiences of our bodies, rooted in locomotion, posture and rhythm, are introjected from material culture. ... the body itself is an artifact, at once created and received by each person in the activity of growing up. Despite its "natural" origin, every aspect of our experience and use of our bodies is saturated with material culture.

findings.consequent: Missing them, discomfort (without conscious awareness of absence)
findings.quote: Environmental constancies may become so familiar that when they disappear, we miss them, even though we have no conscious awareness of an absence, or of what we miss.

findings.antecedent: Removal of habituated train noise (environmental constancy)
findings.consequent: Reports of odd late-night occurrences and discomfort, attributed to nonexistent causes (missing the train noise)
findings.quote: Karl Pribram reported on the "Bowery El" effect. A noisy, late-night, elevated train which ran regularly for years through a New York City neighborhood was stopped and its tracks torn down. At once, people in the neighborhood began to report all manner of odd late-night occurrences, such as thieves, noises and other discomfitures. Investigation revealed that they were missing their train noise; its absence made them uncomfortable, and they attributed their discomfort to nonexistent causes.

findings.consequent: Increasing derivation of habituated environmental elements from material culture
findings.quote: Increasingly, the elements of our environment we habituate derive from material culture.

findings.consequent: Simplified perception, abstraction of environmental structures, problem-solving/prediction (without conscious thought)
findings.quote: implicit (or tacit) processes proceed essentially without direction from or awareness of conscious (or explicit) thought, although the learning, once it has occurred, may provide information or know-how for consciousness. ... Implicit learning and tacit knowledge are abstract and reflect actual environmental structures. Tacit knowledge is used to solve problems, predict events and respond successfully to novel circumstances-all unconsciously!

findings.consequent: Vast majority of human knowledge, core of universal phenomena like language acquisition and socialization
findings.quote: Implicit knowledge processes are responsible for the vast majority of human (and, of course, animal) knowledge; it is out of implicit knowledge that conscious knowledge is explicated. Tacit processes lie at the core of universal phenomena, such as language acquisition and socialization, and also of complex adult learning, such as literary criticism.

findings.consequent: Induction into explicit universes of meaning (fundamental beliefs about existence, time, space, human nature)
findings.quote: Clearly, tacit learning applies to the child's induction into explicit universes of meaning containing fundamental beliefs and experiences about the basic nature of existence and its primary structures such as time, space and human nature, including the body.

findings.consequent: Highly selective screen (designating attention/ignorance), world structuring, protection from 'information overload'
findings.quote: One of the functions of culture is to provide a highly selective screen between man [sic] and the outside world. In its many forms, culture therefore designates what we pay attention to and what we ignore. This screening function provides structure for the world and protects the nervous system from "information overload."

findings.consequent: Differential information screening/attention, stable perceptual patterns throughout life
findings.quote: People brought up in different cultures learn as children, without ever knowing that they have done so, to screen out one type of information while paying close attention to another. Once set, these perceptual patterns apparently remain quite stable throughout life.

findings.consequent: Different screening patterns (visual vs. acoustic), different comfort levels with acoustic environments (Japanese content with paper walls as acoustic screens, Germans/Dutch need thick walls for sound screening and have difficulty concentrating without them)
findings.quote: The Japanese, for example, screen visually in a variety of ways but are perfectly content with paper walls as acoustic screens. Spending the night at a Japanese inn while a party is going on next door is a new sensory experience for the Westerner. In contrast, the Germans and Dutch depend on thick walls and double doors to screen sound, and have difficulty if they must rely on their own powers of concentration to screen out sound.

findings.consequent: Differences in optical illusion perception (many illusions common to Euro-Americans did not appear in other cultures)
findings.quote: Culturally induced differences in perception manifest themselves in the most rudimentary perceptual phenomena such as the optical illusions with which Euro-Americans are all familiar. When Segall, Campbell and Herskovits conducted a series of experiments on the cross-cultural "perception" of illusions, they were surprised to discover that many illusions common to our cultural trajectory did not appear in others.

findings.consequent: Outweighing of individual differences within cultures
findings.quote: They concluded that cultural effects on perception were sufficiently profound to outweigh individual differences within cultures.

findings.antecedent: Built world structural organization (e.g., 'carpentered' vs. rounded shapes), habitual interaction
findings.consequent: Perceptual inference habits, cultural differences in perception
findings.quote: Attributing some of the cause to material culture and some to differences in natural environments, they concluded: "to a substantial extent we learn to perceive... by perceptual inference habits... [that] are differentially likely in different societies." ... The most salient factor they could find was whether the cultural landscape was built around right angles (what they called "carpentered") or whether it took some other principle (for example, the rounded shapes of Mande architecture discussed above).

findings.consequent: Varied experiential importance of different sense modalities ('sense ratios'), differential attention to sensory information
findings.quote: The experiential importance of different sense modalities varies culturally, as well, giving rise to different "sense ratios," as people attend more and less to various sorts of sensory information.

findings.consequent: Sound as predominant sense, organizing primary experience of the world (much as sight does in Euro-America)
findings.quote: to Ellen Basso, among the Kalapalo of the Amazon basin sound is the predominant sense, making evident and organizing the primary experience of the world, much as sight does in our own tradition.

findings.consequent: Different predominant senses (sight dominates in Euro-America; scent dominates in Ommura, 'nose is the window on the soul')
findings.quote: In Euro-America, sight dominates the other senses, while among the Ommura scent predominates the nose is the "window on the soul," not the eyes.

findings.antecedent: Suppression of scent in Euro-American culture
findings.consequent: Uniquely Western experience of individuality, radical simplification of the olfactory spectrum
findings.quote: In our culture, scent is largely suppressed, a fact that seems causally linked to the uniquely Western experience of individuality; the radical simplification of the olfactory spectrum in the West coincided with the rise of our experience of separate and discrete individuals.

findings.consequent: Socio-physiological individuation, privatization of the body, literal distancing from body functions (beginning 16th century)
findings.quote: Socio-physiological individuation began in the 16th century, as the body began to be privatized. People became literally distanced from the body and its functions by means of new paraphernalia of material culture: "table cutlery, handkerchiefs, commodes, nightwear, spittoons, etc." put tools and other artifacts between people and their bodies.

findings.antecedent: Deodorization, suppression of public odor (historical trend, mid-1700s European upper classes to middle class)
findings.consequent: Heightened individuation
findings.quote: The process was heightened and intensified by deodorization and suppression of odor in public which began among the European upper classes in the mid-1700s. It was soon adopted and then universally enforced by the developing middle class.

findings.consequent: Connection at logical, psychological (odors affect memory/reason), and sociological levels (smells synchronize emotional/physical states)
findings.quote: [T]here is a connection between olfaction and transition. between smell and cognitive transformation [at] the logical level (smells are most noticeable at boundaries), the psychological level (given the effect of odours on memory and discursive reason), and the sociological level (smells synchronize the emotional and physical states of the members of a congregation).

findings.consequent: Suppressed transition, stabilized subjective individuals with impermeable boundaries, negated olfactory mediation between selves
findings.quote: By suppressing odor European culture suppressed transition and stabilized the experience of subjective individuals with impermeable boundaries and radical separation from other selves. The elimination of body odors completed the process of individuation begun with the Renaissance social tool kit, "negating any mediation between your self and my self at the olfactory level [so that we] appear to each other as separate (and discreet) individuals."

findings.consequent: Vital role of smell (e.g., marriage partners rejected for 'bad' scent indicating anger/dissatisfaction, denying breath to a friend is shameful)
findings.quote: Among Arabs the presence of smell (rather than its absence) plays a vital role. A marriage partner may be rejected for smelling bad, not because of hygiene, but because of the scent of anger or dissatisfaction, while it is common practice for Arabs to immerse others in breath. For an American, this is both rude and unpleasant. An American doesn't want to smell anyone's breath except perhaps that of a potential sexual partner, while for an Arab, to deny a friend your breath is to act ashamed.

findings.consequent: Essentiality of staying inside the olfactory zone for emotional monitoring
findings.quote: "The Arab finds it essential to stay inside the olfactory zone as a means of keeping tab on changes in emotion."

findings.consequent: Person synonymous with individual inside skin, inviolate skin/clothes, touch requiring permission
findings.quote: In the Western world, the person is synonymous with an individual inside a skin. And in northern Europe generally, the skin and even the clothes may be inviolate. You need permission to touch either if you are a stranger.

findings.consequent: Locus of person 'somewhere down inside the body,' reachable by words (differing from Western locus)
findings.quote: For the Arab the location of the person in relation to the body is quite different. The person exists somewhere down inside the body. [Although it can be reached easily by words.]

findings.antecedent: Gender, age cohort, social status (within a culture)
findings.consequent: Varied sense ratios, sense-meanings, and preferred senses
findings.quote: Sense ratios, sense-meanings, and preferred senses may vary internally within a culture, differing along lines of cultural significance such as gender, age cohort or social status.

findings.consequent: Differential sensory attention (Desana women-touch, men-sight; Western men prefer sight, women prefer touch)
findings.quote: among the Desana, women attend more to touch, while men attend more to sight. Luce Irigaray, a French feminist critic and philosopher, suggests a similar dichotomy in the contemporary West where men prefer sight, with its potential for dominating a scene with a single glance, while women prefer touch with its particularizing, individualizing and localizing tendencies.

findings.consequent: Age-dependent sensory emphasis (young children taught to emphasize touch/taste; older children taught to revile former desires, developing sight/hearing)
findings.quote: Among the Inuit, for example, young children are taught to emphasize touch and taste, but older children are taught to revile what was formerly desired and pleasurable, as they develop instead the senses of sight and especially hearing.

findings.consequent: Experiences of time, space, and the actuality, being, and character of our bodies
findings.quote: Cultural learning at the perceptual level also affects our experiences of time and space and of the actuality, being and character of our bodies.

findings.consequent: Experience of time as a characteristic sequence of events (what happens when corn matures or sheep grows up), alterable by circumstances (not duration or quantity)
findings.quote: [T]he Hopi are separated from us by a tremendous cultural gulf. Time, for example, is not duration but many different things for them. It is not fixed or measurable. nor is it a quantity. It is what happens when the corn matures or a sheep grows up-a characteristic sequence of events. It is the natural process that takes place while living substance acts out its life drama. Therefore, there is a different time for everything which can be altered by circumstances.

findings.consequent: Profound transformation of European body/space, bringing forth spatiality rooted in the experience of 'object' (human bodies as skin bags, consciousness encountering objects horizontally)
findings.quote: European body/space underwent a profound transformation during the Renaissance, bringing forth a spatiality that still predominates in Eurocentric cultures today. It is rooted in the experience of "object": human bodies are experienced as thing-like skin bags inhabited by a nonthing-like "consciousness"; this consciousness, from its embodied perspective (which it struggles to overcome on behalf of a transcendental overview) encounters other objects which are horizontally "over against it" in a rationally organized, perspectival space.

findings.consequent: Vertical spatial organization (earthly realm between heavenly/hellish), 'things' experienced as signs/symbols (not objects)
findings.quote: Medieval space was not organized horizontally, as was the Renaissance space which replaced it, but vertically. The earthly realm was experienced as existing between the heavenly realm (inhabited by the divine) and the hellish realm (inhabited by the demonic). Under some circumstances divine or demonic energy or beings could enter the human, earthly world where most "things" were not experienced as objects, but as signs or symbols within the great "book of the world" of which God was the author.

findings.consequent: Icon meant to create vertical opening into divinity (sacred power into worshipper's soul), human body as imago Dei (not an object)
findings.quote: An icon, for instance, was not meant to depict the earthly reality of the saint or divine figure it represented. Rather, it was intended to create a vertical opening, by means of the sacred power of its subject, into the heart of divinity; through this portal divine energy could pour into the soul of the worshipper. ... For the Medieval world, the human body was not an object, but an imago Dei, whose form was the soul and which comprised the battleground between demonic and divine.

findings.consequent: Everything exists in the horizontal dimension, art becomes an artifact for aesthetic appreciation/analytical investigation
findings.quote: In Renaissance space, on the other hand, everything exists in the horizontal dimension. Even the sun and the stars are in the "same" space as the human body; verticality is horizontality stood on end. A work of art becomes an artifact, not an icon. It is intended to depict its subjects with a convincing illusion of earthly reality. It is an object inviting aesthetic appreciation and analytical investigation.

findings.consequent: Viewer distancing from artifact, standing apart as if looking through a window, to capture scene with dominating gaze (for clarity/insight)
findings.quote: To view a Renaissance painting one must distance one's body from the artifact, standing apart as if looking through a window, in order to capture the presented scene in a dominating gaze with clarity and insight.

findings.consequent: Uniform mathematical analysis of space, experience of seemingly consistent and rational perception
findings.quote: Renaissance painters began this spatial transformation with the vanishing-point perspective through which they achieved the first uniform mathematical analysis of space. Using this mathematical analysis they could create the experience of a seemingly consistent and rational perception

findings.antecedent: Abstract spatial construction (perspective) applied to built environments (city squares, private estates)
findings.consequent: Eventually vanished and replaced by a sense of 'natural' space
findings.quote: Soon this abstract spatial construction was applied to the design of city squares, then to private estates, and then to the organization of larger and larger units of design ... Any awareness that this space was constructed eventually vanished and was replaced with a sense that it was "natural" space.

findings.antecedent: Separation of viewer from view, objectification of both
findings.consequent: Experience of space, things in the world taking on status of objects with definite boundaries
findings.quote: This experience of space depends on the separation of the viewer from the view, and of the objectification of both. The body, as well as things in the world, take on the status of objects, with definite boundaries and clear, oppositional relationships.

findings.consequent: Representation of eternity in four forms (mathematical ordering, human mind's comprehension, human power to structure nature, imperial control)
findings.quote: This space reached its apotheosis in the gardens of Versailles, where it simultaneously represents eternity in four forms: the mathematical ordering of the universe, the human mind's ability to comprehend this order, human power to structure nature accordingly, and imperial power viewed as a totalizing control of central authority over both nature and subject people.

findings.consequent: Privilege of interval (ma), originating in liminal moment when kami appeared, valuing flowing, transient, simple, 'empty' character of things
findings.quote: traditional Japanese culture privileges interval (ma), which is held to originate in the liminal moment when kami (Shinto sacred power) appeared. ... While the ma sensitivity has manifested itself throughout Japanese culture, for the most part it can be seen in an aesthetic of form that values the flowing, processing, transforming, transient, ephemeral, subdued, simple, clean, and "empty" character of things.

findings.consequent: Introduction of time element into their design ('gardens of time'), contrasting with Western landscaping that makes monuments invalid if time is introduced
findings.quote: I call Japanese gardens "gardens of time" . [On the other hand] It never occurred to the Western art of landscaping to introduce the element of time into its gardens. And if this element had been introduced, it would have eroded the forms, destroyed the order, and made the monuments invalid.

findings.consequent: Pleasure from 'seeing a crystal-clear world in which nothing is deliberately concealed, in which every nook and corner is analyzed, comprehended, ordered and integrated'
findings.quote: Versailles seems, to Mishima's Japanese sensibility, designed to give the incomparable pleasure that comes from "seeing a crystal-clear world in which nothing is deliberately concealed, in which every nook and corner is analyzed, comprehended, ordered and integrated."

findings.consequent: No trace of human effort except in overall plan, acknowledging nature's transforming power, blending human intention with natural occurrence
findings.quote: Shugaku-in "was intended to show no trace of human effort except in the overall plan." Here the goal is to acknowledge the transforming power of time and to blend human intention with natural occurrence so that the two cannot be extricated from one another.

findings.consequent: Rhythmicized/temporalized body/space experience (Japanese) vs. space apart from time and body removed from its temporality (Renaissance)
findings.quote: The Japanese have rhythmicized and temporalized the experience of body/space; in the Renaissance tradition space has been held apart from time and the body removed from its own temporality.

findings.antecedent: European-derived experience of bodies as things
findings.consequent: Philosophical problem of reconciling 'subjectivity' of awareness with 'objectivity' of embodiment
findings.quote: Our European-derived tendency to experience our bodies as things generates the great philosophical problem of reconciling the "subjectivity" of our awareness with the "objectivity" of our embodiment.

findings.consequent: Dynamic experience of the body (as capacity for transforming ma in an ever fluid and changing pattern)
findings.quote: From the Japanese context the body may be experienced dynamically, as the capacity for transforming ma in an ever fluid and changing pattern.

findings.consequent: Accustomed experience of the world 'laid out' in front of bodies (especially eyes), with objective of comprehensive view
findings.quote: in the post-Renaissance West we are accustomed to experiencing the world "laid out" in front of our bodies, especially our eyes. Our objective is to have a comprehensive view, with either a glance or a penetrating gaze.

findings.consequent: Overall, unconscious, automatic approach to the coherence of the world
findings.quote: Culture affects our overall, unconscious, automatic approach to the coherence of the world.

findings.consequent: Different learning styles, different conceptual boundaries ('where to draw the line separating one thing from another')
findings.quote: People reared in different cultures "learn to learn differently." "Culture has always dictated where to draw the line separating one thing from another."

findings.consequent: Different apprehension of 'individual' (single person vs. kin group)
findings.quote: In the West we experience a person surrounded by a skin and supported by bones and a nervous system, all of which is apprehended as a single and individual thing, a human being. But for the Pueblo Indians, a kin group resembling a lineage is experienced as the single individual, and the people are experienced as "parts".

findings.consequent: Different 'logics' (conscious/semiconscious explications of tacit structures shaping worlds), corresponding to underlying perceptual structures
findings.quote: Cultures enact different "logics," which are conscious or semiconscious explications of the tacit structures which shape their worlds. These logics emerge from and correspond to the perceptual structures that underlie experience.

findings.consequent: Structured body/world, permeated with implicitly learned patterns, explicated in formal knowledge systems (e.g., science)
findings.quote: Throughout this essay we have seen how material culture structures the body/world, permeating it with implicitly learned patterns. Structures which are explicated in formal systems of knowledge map tacit patterns generated through the variety of means we have examined above.

findings.consequent: Cultural differences in science ('Sushi Science and Hamburger Science'), behavior, talk, and thought
findings.quote: Japanese biologist Tatsuo Motokawa to write "Sushi Science and Hamburger Science," an instructive essay on the cultural differences between Western and Japanese science. Describing his experience as a visiting scientist at Duke University, Motokawa noted: What struck me most is the difference in the behavior of the people. The way they talk, the way they think, the way they laugh, the way they express their anger-all are different from those I have been used to. The daily experiences and observations of these differences have led me to notice that there exist some differences in science and the way it is done.

findings.consequent: Mind-body integration, 'real fact' from observation/experiment (avoiding interpretation)
findings.quote: Mind and body should go hand in hand in Eastern science. There is a real fact in front of you. You can obtain it if you stop speaking and devote yourself to the observations and experiments to the extent that you become unaware that you are observing or doing experiments. To interpret is to create your personal world, which always closes the way to the truth.

findings.consequent: Fact becomes truth only after interpretation as part of a universal rule
findings.quote: [whereas in Western science] the fact becomes a truth only after it has been interpreted as a part of a universal rule.

findings.consequent: Focus on 'ma' (intervals) between facts, describing things from many non-logically connected points of view
findings.quote: Japanese scientific talk focuses attention on the gaps (intervals-ma) between facts. It works to describe things from many points of view which are not logically connected.

findings.consequent: Perceived as aggressive and false by Japanese (as words can never be absolutely true)
findings.quote: Japanese may find the Western scientist's habit of stating conclusions both aggressive and false: "... if we state a conclusion, it means that our statement is the truth. Such a statement is definitely false because our words can never be absolutely true."

findings.antecedent: Perceptual structuring (cultural, material culture, tacit knowledge)
findings.consequent: Affected dimensions of experience and behavior
findings.quote: This contrast between Japanese and Euro-American science, as well as the existence of culturally varied logics, demonstrates that differences in perceptual structuring, tied to varying material cultures and embedded in tacit knowledge, affect every dimension of experience and behavior, including the most abstract and seemingly universal.

findings.consequent: Brain coding of knowledge, different ways of thinking
findings.quote: Recent evidence in cognitive neuropsychology indicates that knowledge is coded in the brain according to the modality of experience. "It follows that insofar as different cultures emphasize the development of different modalities, their ways of thinking will also differ."

findings.consequent: Different sensory experience of the world (looks, smells, tastes different)
findings.quote: The world literally looks, smells and tastes different to people from differing ethnicities and cultures.

findings.consequent: Different arrangements and significances, creating a very different structure to life
findings.quote: More importantly, the sights and tastes and smells are put together into different arrangements and significances, creating a very different structure to life.

findings.consequent: Drawing lines between things (reality/fantasy), arbitrary lines experienced as real once learned and internalized
findings.quote: Developmental learning indicates where to draw the line separating one thing from another-including reality from fantasy. These lines are somewhat arbitrary, but once learned and internalized they are experienced as real

findings.consequent: Different sensory worlds, different worlds to think about, different ways of thinking
findings.quote: people from different cultures "inhabit different sensory worlds." Not only do people with different sense ratios think differently about the world, people with different sense ratios have different worlds about which to think!

findings.consequent: Hominid perceptual system evolution, enculturation as natural selection factor (material from the outset)
findings.quote: The evolution of hominid perceptual systems has emerged under the influence of material culture over an extensive period of time. The ability to enculturate has itself been a factor in natural selection in human evolution, and enculturation has been material from the outset.

findings.consequent: Radically unfinished newborn, requirement for shared perceptual/cognitive worlds (generated/maintained by material culture) for survival
findings.quote: Hominid evolution engendered species needing cooperative and coordinated social activity for individual and collective survival. As part of this process an extended neoteny developed, creating both a radically unfinished newborn and a necessarily extended interaction between adults and children. Survival in this setting required shared perceptual and cognitive worlds, which were themselves generated and maintained by means of material culture.

findings.consequent: Culturally variable human perception (since 2,000,000-750,000 years ago)
findings.quote: From this point onward human perception has been culturally variable, and this variability has been largely determined by the artifacts and processes of material culture.

findings.consequent: Body as cultural artifact, meaning (somatic feeling, imaged meaning) given by cultural environment
findings.quote: The body, as experienced, is a cultural artifact, whose meaning, both as somatic feeling and as imaged meaning, are given by the cultural environment of the infant, primarily through the experience of material culture.

findings.consequent: Deeply felt sense of 'the way things are,' forming fundamental basis for evaluations of worth/appropriateness/significance
findings.quote: Temporality, spatiality and gender are inherently involved in this bodily construction. They carry with them a deeply felt sense of "the way things are" which forms a fundamental basis for evaluations of worth, appropriateness and significance.

findings.consequent: Evaluations seeming natural/eternal but are constructed/circumstantial; perception is profoundly mediated
findings.quote: These evaluations, rooted in apparently "immediate" perceptual experience, seem natural and eternal but are in fact constructed and circumstantial. Although perception seems to be immediate, it is in fact profoundly mediated.

findings.consequent: Inherently dramatic, dynamic, and processual experience, with sacramental mid-point (altar) and nave as path to sanctuary
findings.quote: Christian space is inherently dramatic, dynamic and processual, in keeping with the dynamism that lies at the heart of the Christian revelation. This space, first realized and most fully symbolized in the cathedral, permeates the development of space in the European trajectory. Writes Titus Burckhardt: A church has a sacramental mid-point, the altar, toward which everything converges; the choir is the sanctuary sheltering the altar, and the nave is like a path leading from the outer world towards this sanctuary; when the church is divided into narthex, nave and choir, it bespeaks a hierarchy of approach to the sacred.

findings.consequent: Essentially static and non-dynamic experience, no sacred center, reabsorbed into ubiquity of present moment, suggesting no tension between here-below/beyond
findings.quote: the mosque has no sacred centre within its walls the space within a mosque is like a segment of one of the innumerable concentric circles surrounding the sanctuary at Mecca. [there is an] essentially static and non-dynamic conception of space, in the state of equilibrium and repose that Islamic architecture expresses in all its forms. The space, of which it communicates the experience, is as if reabsorbed into the ubiquity of the present moment; it does not beckon the eye in a specific direction; it suggests no tension or antinomy as between the here-below and the beyond, or between earth and heaven; it possesses all its fullness in every place.

findings.consequent: 'Uses of space' (e.g., Christian/Islamic) derived from and correlated with enculturated bodies
findings.quote: These "uses of space" derive from distinctive experiences of space, and these experiences are correlated with the enculturated bodies of those whose experiences they are.

findings.consequent: Many distinctive cultural spatialities, distinguishable by visual terms and primary sensory modality (olfactory, auditory, kinaesthetic) used to experience space
findings.quote: There is substantial and mounting evidence that there are many distinctive cultural spatialities, which can be distinguished not only in visual terms, but also by means of the primary sensory modality used to experience space, which, after all, has olfactory, auditory and kinaesthetic sources that are at least as profound as the visual.

limitations: Limning the history of perception is a dicey task. Historical artifacts and texts give evidence of bygone perceptual reality, but what people said about their perceptions, and our interpretations of the material culture that engendered and reflected those perceptions, are equivocal evidence as to how they actually perceived. (p. 3)
It is not easy to think through the role of culture in perceptual difference. (p. 3)
Culture is an increasingly slippery concept with which to work. (p. 14, footnote 24)
minimum_safe_summary: This theoretical paper argues that human perception is profoundly shaped by culture and history, with material culture playing a central role in this process. It posits that the body itself is a primary artifact of material culture, influencing how individuals perceive and interact with their environment. Key findings include cross-cultural variations in sensory dominance (e.g., sight in the West vs. smell/sound in other cultures), the impact of architectural forms on social organization, and how implicit learning and habituation to material environments shape our fundamental understanding of time, space, and self. The paper highlights that these culturally mediated perceptual patterns are deeply embedded and often unconscious, leading to genuinely different "sensory worlds" across cultures. Acknowledged limitations include the inherent difficulty in reconstructing past perceptual realities from historical artifacts and texts.
